reason: The sources provide 16 robust, cross-verified claims detailing the discovery, scale, mapping technique, naming, and ultimate fate of the Laniakea Supercluster.
story: For generations, we thought our cosmic neighborhood ended at the edge of the Milky Way, or perhaps our local group of galaxies. But in September 2014, astronomers mapping the heavens made a mind-bending discovery. Our home galaxy is just a tiny speck inside a newly mapped, colossal supercluster named Laniakea—Hawaiian for 'immense heaven.' Spanning up to 500 million light-years and packed with the mass of 100 quadrillion Suns, this cosmic web binds 100,000 galaxies together. To map it, scientists didn't just look at where galaxies are; they tracked how they move. They discovered that all 100,000 galaxies are sliding along gravitational pathways, like water flowing down a valley, toward a mysterious focal point called the Great Attractor. Yet, this titanic structure is not permanent. Dark energy is actively pulling Laniakea apart, meaning our 'immense heaven' will eventually dissolve into the void.
angle: Our galaxy belongs to a mapped 100,000-galaxy supercluster where we are all sliding like water down a valley toward a cosmic focal point, but dark energy will eventually tear it apart.

claims.claim: The Laniakea Supercluster was mapped and defined in September 2014.
The name Laniakea means 'immense heaven' or 'open skies' in Hawaiian.
The name Laniakea was suggested by Nawaʻa Napoleon, a language professor at Kapiʻolani Community College.
The name honors Polynesian navigators who used knowledge of the heavens to navigate across the Pacific Ocean.
Our home galaxy, the Milky Way, is located in the outskirts of the Laniakea Supercluster.
The structure spans roughly 400 million to 500 million light-years in diameter.
Laniakea has an approximate mass of 10^17 (100 quadrillion) solar masses.
The astronomical team that defined Laniakea was led by R. Brent Tully of the University of Hawaii.
The researchers mapped the supercluster using galaxy movements and peculiar velocities instead of just light-based positions.
Within Laniakea, galaxy motions are directed inward toward a central region of mass.
The central gravitational focal point of Laniakea is known as the Great Attractor.
Laniakea is moving toward a much larger neighboring structure called the Shapley Concentration.
The Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia was among the key radio telescopes used to map the velocities of these galaxies.
The scientific paper was published as the cover story of the journal Nature in September 2014.
Galactic motion inside the boundaries of Laniakea is compared to water flowing down a valley.

disputed: The physical size of Laniakea: S1 cites roughly 400 million light-years, while S3, S4, and S7 cite 500 million light-years. A script should use '400 to 500 million light-years' to remain accurate.

The definition and permanence of Laniakea: While originally defined as a supercluster, subsequent studies suggest it is not gravitationally bound and will be torn apart by dark energy, prompting some astronomers to call it a 'supercluster cocoon' or 'basin of attraction'. A script should mention that Laniakea is projected to dissolve in the far future.
